w: Momofuku Ando invented instant ramen in a backyard shed on this exact Ikeda plot in 1958. The museum built on the site lets visitors design their own cup noodle flavor and packaging on a working assembly line, beside a recreated version of Ando's shed and decades of noodle brands sold worldwide.
s: Where instant ramen was invented, in Ando's shed
why: Birthplace museum of instant noodles, with a make-your-own noodle line

w: A private museum built by physician Satoru Kamegai around his own research collection, now holding some 60,000 parasite specimens. Its star exhibit is an 8.8-metre tapeworm pulled from a human intestine, unspooled to full length. Admission is free; the gift shop sells parasite-themed neckties.
s: 60,000 parasites, one 8.8m tapeworm on display
why: World's only parasite-only museum, founded by one obsessive doctor

w: Started by a divorcing couple unsure what to do with the shared belongings of their relationship, this collection holds thousands of donated breakup objects, each with a short anonymous note on what it meant and why it ended. An axe used to chop up an ex's furniture sits under glass as a monument to heartbreak.
s: Breakup objects and the stories behind them
why: Crowdsourced museum of heartbreak that spawned a global franchise

w: Assistant attorney general Barry Levenson began collecting mustard jars in 1986 after the Red Sox blew the World Series, and the hobby grew into a roadside institution holding over 6,000 mustards from 70-plus countries. Free tastings run from a refrigerated case, and the gift shop sells mustard ice cream.
s: 6,000 jars of mustard, free tastings included
why: World's largest mustard collection, born from a bad baseball loss

w: Founded by lawnmower racer and restorer Brian Radam, this shop-front museum traces two centuries of grass-cutting technology, from Edwin Budding's 1830 patent to a mower once owned by Prince Charles. Vintage racing mowers and steam-powered cutters fill the cramped display, tribute to a very British obsession.
s: Two centuries of lawnmowers, including royal ones
why: Only museum in the world devoted purely to lawnmowers

w: Sanitation reformer Bindeshwar Pathak built this museum to make toilet history impossible to ignore, tracing 4,500 years of latrines from Harappan drainage systems to Louis XIV's velvet commode chair and a Victorian toilet disguised as a bookcase, underpinning Sulabh's public-toilet movement across India.
s: 4,500 years of toilets, from Harappa to Versailles
why: Serious sanitation-history museum wrapped around a bathroom-humor collection

w: Sited near Potsdamer Platz, this museum walks visitors through espionage tradecraft from ancient ciphers to Cold War Berlin, the front line of East-West spying. Exhibits include a shoe with a hidden heel transmitter, lipstick pistols, an Enigma machine, and a laser maze to cross without triggering an alarm.
s: Cold War tradecraft, Enigma machines, a laser maze
why: Deep single-subject dive into spy history in the city that spied on itself

w: Run by law firm Tilleke and Gibbins inside its own office tower, this appointment-only collection of some 4,000 fakes pairs counterfeit handbags, watches, and pharmaceuticals against their genuine counterparts. Assembled from decades of intellectual-property casework, it doubles as a training tool for investigators.
s: 4,000 fakes, shown side by side with the real thing
why: Law firm's private trove of counterfeits, open by appointment only

w: Founded by a retired teacher who received a bull's pizzle as a joke gift, this collection holds specimens from nearly every mammal in Iceland, including a legally donated human one. Whale and walrus specimens sit in formaldehyde jars beside phallus-shaped folk art, treated with straight-faced seriousness.
s: Penises from nearly every Icelandic mammal, plus one human
why: Probably the only museum on Earth built entirely around phallic specimens

w: Kotor's Old Town has fed and sheltered stray cats for centuries, crediting them with saving the medieval city's grain stores from rats. This small museum catalogues that obsession with feline postcards, engravings, and paintings dating to the 1800s. Outside, actual cats still roam the marble streets as mascots.
s: Centuries of cat art from a city that worships strays
why: Only museum dedicated to the cats of one specific Adriatic town

w: Visitors descend a working section of the 19th-century sewer network engineered under Baron Haussmann's Paris, walking galleries named for the streets above while sluice gates and giant wooden cleaning tools demonstrate two centuries of wastewater engineering, plus a nod to Victor Hugo's sewer chase in Les Miserables.
s: Walk a real sewer tunnel beneath the Seine
why: Working sewer network turned into a walkable engineering museum

w: Sited inside Vienna's vast Central Cemetery, this museum unpacks the city's cult of the beautiful corpse, a baroque obsession with elaborate funerals, mourning fashion, and hearses. A reusable coffin with a trapdoor bottom, built under Emperor Joseph II to save costs, sits beside a bell-rigged safety coffin.
s: Reusable coffins and bell-rigged safety caskets
why: Vienna's obsessive death culture distilled into one graveyard museum

w: Donated to Leeds Castle in 1977 by collector Gertrude Hunt, this collection spans five centuries of dog collars, from spiked medieval iron bands built to protect hunting dogs from wolf bites to gilded Tudor pieces and jewel-studded Victorian show collars, displayed inside the castle's former kennels.
s: 500 years of dog collars, from wolf-spikes to jewels
why: Niche 500-year survey of one accessory, inside a medieval castle

w: Potter Chez Galip began this collection in 1979 after a friend moved away, keeping a lock of her hair in his cave workshop; word spread and thousands of women visiting Avanos began leaving their own locks, each pinned with a name and address. More than 16,000 hair samples now cover the cave walls and ceiling.
s: 16,000 women's hair locks pinned to cave walls
why: Accidental collection that grew into a record-holding hair archive

w: Founded in 1951 by occultist Cecil Williamson, this harbourside museum holds the world's largest collection of witchcraft artefacts, from ritual skulls and poppets to Aleister Crowley's tarot deck and spell books used in English cunning-folk practice. It survived a 2004 flood that nearly destroyed the collection.
s: World's largest witchcraft and magic artefact archive
why: Serious occult-history museum built from one collector's lifelong obsession

w: Insurance executive William Shakespeare Berger began collecting ventriloquist figures in the 1910s, and his hobby grew into the only museum in the world devoted to ventriloquism, now holding over 1,000 dummies once worked by Edgar Bergen and Paul Winchell. Three buildings seat the figures in rows on old church pews.
s: Over 1,000 silent ventriloquist dummies on pews
why: World's only museum devoted entirely to ventriloquism

w: Hormel Foods built this museum in its hometown to celebrate the canned meat it introduced in 1937 and shipped by the hundreds of millions of cans to feed Allied troops in WWII. Interactive exhibits include a canning-line race game and a wall of international flavor variants.
s: Canned-meat history, with a can-packing race game
why: Corporate hometown museum devoted to one specific canned meat

w: Overlooking Amsterdam's flower market, this museum displays more than 40 authentic instruments of judicial torture and execution used across medieval Europe, from thumbscrews and the rack to a scold's bridle worn to publicly shame gossiping women. Wall texts explain the legal reasoning once used to justify each device.
s: 40+ genuine instruments of medieval judicial torture
why: Single-subject collection of Europe's actual torture and execution tools

w: Gignese once supplied much of Europe with hand-made umbrellas, and this two-story museum, shaped like three overlapping umbrellas, preserves that trade with roughly 1,500 pieces spanning Napoleonic-era parasols to Belle Epoque folding umbrellas with carved ivory handles carried across the Alps by itinerant menders.
s: 1,500 umbrellas in a building shaped like three of them
why: Village-industry museum for a craft almost nobody else preserves

w: Tucked into La Paz's Witches' Market district, this small museum lays out the coca leaf's role in Andean life over 4,000 years, from ceremonial offerings and chewing to its industrial extraction into cocaine. Period pharmacy bottles of coca tonics and early Coca-Cola ads sit alongside exhibits on the drug trade.
s: 4,000 years of coca leaf, sacred plant to cocaine
why: Single-plant museum spanning Andean ritual and the global drug trade

w: La Crosse calls itself the Barbed Wire Capital of the World, and this museum backs the claim with more than 2,000 distinct wire patterns patented from the 1870s onward, alongside the hand tools used to string fence across the Great Plains. Exhibits explain how barbed wire ended the open range and sparked range wars.
s: 2,000+ barbed wire patterns that fenced the prairie
why: Only accredited museum devoted purely to barbed wire

w: Former Suwon mayor Sim Jae-duck, nicknamed Mr. Toilet for his sanitation advocacy, had his own house built in the shape of a toilet bowl and willed it to the city as a museum on his death in 2009. Surrounding gardens display sculptures on toilet history, tied to Sim's founding of the World Toilet Association.
s: A house shaped like a toilet, built by 'Mr. Toilet'
why: Sanitation activist's own toilet-shaped home turned into a museum

w: Spread across six floors of a private Saigon townhouse, this museum was built by a pharmacist family to preserve Vietnam's herbal medicine tradition, displaying thousands of dried herbs, apothecary drawers, mortars, and antique cabinets. A rooftop garden traces the trade from court physicians to street herbalists.
s: Six floors of herbs, mortars, and apothecary drawers
why: Private family museum preserving Vietnam's herbal medicine trade

w: Built to train UNSW medical students, this museum displays several thousand real human tissue specimens showing disease's physical effects, from tumours and cirrhotic livers to smoker's lungs and a case of leprosy. Open to the public despite its clinical origins, it presents pathology in unfiltered detail.
s: Thousands of real diseased human organs on display
why: Medical-school specimen collection opened to the curious public

w: Nobel laureate Orhan Pamuk built this museum as a companion to his novel of the same name, filling 83 display cases, one per chapter, with objects from an obsessive love affair: cigarette butts, hair clips, restaurant menus, a clock stopped at the moment sorrow began. The novel itself serves as its catalogue.
s: A novel turned into 83 real display cases
why: Only museum built as the literal physical twin of a work of fiction

w: A 19th-century tax on grave plots led Guanajuato's cemetery keepers to disinter unpaid graves, and the region's mineral-rich, arid soil had naturally mummified many of the bodies inside. Over a hundred are now displayed standing upright in glass cases, clothing and expressions frozen from the moment of exhumation.
s: 100+ naturally mummified bodies from unpaid graves
why: Accidental mummies created by burial-tax non-payment, now on display

w: Spread across four floors of an Old Town building, this museum traces mechanical devices built for sexual purposes from Leonardo da Vinci-era sketches through Victorian medical hysteria treatment machines to a 19th-century pedal-powered contraption, presented with academic captions rather than titillation.
s: Four floors of mechanical sex devices since da Vinci
why: Only museum tracing the engineering history of sex machines

w: Built specifically to explain the technical process behind ancient Egyptian mummification rather than just display its results, this Nile-front museum walks through the removal of organs into canopic jars, the 40-day natron drying process, and the wrapping rituals guided by Anubis imagery, alongside embalmers' tools.
s: The technical how-to of ancient Egyptian mummification
why: Single museum devoted entirely to the mummification process itself

w: Retired from the South African Navy in 2003 after 33 years of service, the diesel-electric submarine Assegaai was hauled onto dry land at Simon's Town naval base and converted into Africa's first submarine museum. Visitors squeeze through its torpedo-loading hatch into corridors barely wide enough for two crew to pass.
s: A retired submarine, hauled ashore and walked through
why: Africa's first and only walk-through submarine museum
